entries.title: Zod Brings In-Process Schema Compilation and a 9x Cut in Memory Footprint
entries.summary: Zod is a TypeScript-focused schema validation library that recently released versions 4.5 and 4.6. Key updates include schema compilation for faster data parsing, significant memory usage reductions, and new validation features. The library supports efficient validation processes and remains popular in the JavaScript ecosystem, achieving millions of downloads weekly. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
Zod, the TypeScript-first schema validation library created by Colin McDonnell, released Zod 4.5 on August 28, 2026, introducing schema compilation, an order-of-magnitude cut in schema memory usage, and a batch of long-requested helpers. Zod 4.6 followed on September 9, extending that work and fixing a recursive-schema memory regression. The major compilation and memory-footprint changes arrived in 4.5, which remains the focus here, but developers upgrading now should also account for the subsequent release.

The flagship addition is 

z.compile()
, which turns any schema into a precompiled validator that parses the same data three to nine times faster. The compiled schema behaves exactly like the original, with no special rules. Importantly, as McDonnell explains, compilation happens in-process rather than at build time, so there is no bundler plugin or codegen step to wire up.

Teams that want this applied everywhere can add 

import "zod/compile"
at the top of an entry point, or run 
node --import zod/compile app.js
, after which every schema is compiled lazily the first time it parses data.

By memoising bound methods instead of allocating them per instance, a bare 

z.string()
now retains 784 bytes of heap rather than 7.5kb, a roughly nine-fold reduction. 
safeParse()
also skips stack-trace capture on failure, making invalid input about 7.5 times cheaper to reject. Alongside the speed, 4.5 restores 
z.deepPartial()
, and adds 
.exactPartial()
, 
z.creditCard()
, 
z.input()
/
z.output()
, cyclical data in recursive schemas, and eight new error locales.

The most directly relevant 4.6 addition is 

.validate()
, a boolean-only check that avoids constructing a parsed result or 
ZodError
and can stop at the first issue. With compilation enabled, the release reports up to a 35-fold improvement over 
.safeParse().success
on invalid input—not a general parsing speed-up or a replacement when transformed output or error details are needed.

Version 4.6 also adds property validation on class instances, six additional validation keywords in 

z.fromJSONSchema()
, and 
z.iban()
. For environments whose Content Security Policy blocks the 
new Function
used by 
z.compile()
, 
z.withParser()
can install an externally generated parser; it does not generate that parser itself.

Importantly, 4.6 fixes a 4.5 regression that retained parsed data in recursive schemas and could cause out-of-memory failures.

Developer Mehul Mohan described the roughly tenfold improvement on objects and arrays as "a real performance win".

On the Moltar parseSafe benchmark cited in the release, compiled Zod reaches 47.5M ops/sec, edging ahead of Typia at 45.3M and leaving Valibot (1.8M) and ArkType (152k) far behind, a notable turn given ArkType has long marketed itself as many times faster than Zod. On the boolean-only assertion benchmark published with 4.5, Typia and ArkType led compiled Zod. Those figures remain a snapshot of that release, not a fresh comparison against 4.6's new 

.validate()
path; the fastest option remains workload-dependent.

Moltarbench results from the release article.



Zod is an open-source, TypeScript-first validation library used to define schemas and parse untrusted data with fully inferred static types. It is one of the most widely adopted validation tools in the JavaScript ecosystem, with first-class support across tRPC, React Hook Form, and many backend frameworks, and it now sees more than 30 million weekly downloads.

entries.title: Uber Automates Dependency Analysis Across Its Service Mesh
entries.summary: Uber has developed an automated dependency analysis system that uses RPC middleware and production metrics to correlate caller and downstream failures. The approach classifies dependencies as fail-close, fail-open, or unknown and addresses limitations of sampled distributed tracing for rare failures across Uber’s large service mesh. By Leela Kumili
entries.content:
Uber has developed an automated approach to mapping service dependencies and classifying how downstream failures propagate across its service mesh. The system uses RPC middleware to correlate caller and callee failures across production requests, classifying dependencies as fail-close, fail-open, or unknown. Uber says the approach has cataloged dependencies for critical APIs and indexed most fail-close anomalies across its service mesh.



The Uber Engineering team highlighted the motivation in a LinkedIn post,

When a request fails, how do you figure out what actually caused it? At Uber’s scale, that gets complicated fast. With thousands of services and dependencies interacting, traditional tracing can’t always give engineers the full picture quickly enough.

In a microservices architecture, requests can traverse deeply nested and asynchronous service calls, making it difficult to determine which dependency contributed to a failure. Uber defines a fail-close dependency as one whose failure can consistently cause its caller to fail. A fail-open dependency can fail without causing its caller to fail, while insufficient evidence results in an unknown classification. The classification can then be applied across call paths to identify how failures may propagate toward an originating API.

Uber initially considered distributed tracing for establishing these relationships, but found sampling too slow for rare failures. The company says more than 99.9% of requests complete without errors and within acceptable latency bounds. At a 0.01% sampling rate and 99.9% availability, an erroneous request has a one-in-10-million chance of being sampled. At 500 requests per second, capturing one failed request could therefore take 5 hours, 33 minutes, and 20 seconds.

Uber Engineers Deepanshu Mehndiratta, Alok Srivastava and Shivam Jindal describe the approach as a trade-off between individual request visibility and faster dependency analysis.

We needed something with faster feedback, so we started identifying dependencies through logging.

Uber’s request flow through the Muttley proxy, showing caller and callee communication and telemetry (Source: Uber Blog Post)

Uber routes service-to-service requests through Muttley, an on-host proxy for routing and telemetry. However, Muttley lacks caller endpoint context for precise dependency correlation. Uber added the analysis to YARPC, its RPC framework for Go and Java, using inbound and outbound middleware.

Inbound middleware generates a request ID and records the caller service and endpoint in an in-memory RequestTracker. The ID propagates through Go’s context, enabling Outbound middleware to record the downstream service, endpoint, and call result. At request completion, middleware emits metrics capturing caller and callee failure states.

Complete request flow for mapping inbound and outbound failures (Source: Uber Blog Post)

Uber calculates a failure correlation probability for each caller dependency based on observed caller and callee outcomes. Values ≥0.8 are classified as fail-close, ≤0.2 as fail-open, and intermediate values as unknown. Retries are handled separately to avoid treating them as independent dependencies. Unlike distributed tracing pipelines built with OpenTelemetry, where tail sampling can retain traces based on errors or latency, Uber uses middleware metrics to capture production failures without the overhead of storing and evaluating individual traces, trading request-level detail for broader coverage.

entries.title: AI in Production: Panellists Highlight Silent Failures, Harness Engineering, and Agent Governance
entries.summary: A recent InfoQ webinar examined operational challenges in deploying agentic systems. Key points included issues like semantic and embedding drift, which can lead to significant errors. Experts discussed the need for automated code reviews, continuous evaluation of models, and enhanced privacy measures. The session emphasised a strategic approach to deployment and security management. By Olimpiu Po
entries.content:
During a recent InfoQ webinar titled "AI in Production: What Breaks, What Works, and Who Approves It?", a panel of senior engineering practitioners met to dissect the real-world operational challenges of deploying agentic systems. The discussion was moderated by Hien Luu and featured Zichuan Xiong and Prem Chandrasekaran from ThoughtWorks, privacy specialist Katharine Jarmul, and financial AI practitioner Lan Chu. Luu opened the session by noting three core drivers: AI fails differently from traditional software by generating convincing inaccuracies rather than crashing; coding agents are generating production code faster than humans can review; and sensitive data has new places to leak through prompts, context windows, and retrieved documents.

Xiong, Head of AI Ops for Managed Services at ThoughtWorks, highlighted the widespread issue of "semantic drift" in LLM pipelines. He described how text-to-SQL translation agents frequently flatten domain-specific concepts, such as treating "member" identically across sales and customer support domains, leading to subtle, hidden errors in downstream business analytics that pass standard tracing. Similarly, Chu recounted a critical failure caused by "embedding drift" in financial compliance systems. After deploying an agent to block prohibited investment advice based on vector similarity thresholds, an unannounced background update to the underlying embedding model altered the vector distance distribution. This caused severe false positive and false negative spikes in live traffic while all infrastructure health checks remained completely green. Additionally, Chandrasekaran highlighted how RAG pipelines can inadvertently retrieve sensitive documents, while Jarmul noted that models inherently memorize training data and can be used to de-anonymize information or expose API keys. Chandrasekaran also referenced the GitSpawn vulnerability, showing how malicious repository configurations can execute unauthorized code during routine commands.

As coding assistants generate an increasingly massive volume of production code, conventional human code review processes face unsustainable bottlenecks. Chandrasekaran, Tech and Business Services Lead at ThoughtWorks, emphasized that line-by-line manual code reviews cannot scale alongside high-velocity agent outputs. Instead, engineering teams must automate tactical style and syntax checks within CI/CD pipelines, reserving human oversight strictly for high-level architecture, business intent, and non-functional requirements. Xiong added that teams must shift left to evaluate intent at the harness level before pull requests are generated. Chandrasekaran also highlighted the resurgence of mutation testing as an essential practice. By introducing deliberate code mutations, teams can verify whether automated test suites truly evaluate underlying logic or merely satisfy surface-level code coverage metrics. When evaluating agentic systems, Chu stressed that evals must be treated as permanent, living infrastructure rather than static pre-release checklists. Effective evaluation requires continuous online tracing at the span level, log filtering, and using LLMs to categorize failure patterns, enabling teams to feed production edge cases back into offline benchmark suites.

Effective evaluation requires continuous online tracing at the span level, enabling teams to capture real-world user interaction patterns and systematically feed production edge cases back into offline benchmark suites.

To address privacy and security risks, Jarmul cautioned against relying on prompt engineering for system defence. She advocated for systematic red teaming, continuous threat modeling, defining strict functional scopes for autonomous agents, and scaling observability to handle expanded event volumes. To limit the blast radius of autonomous agent actions, Chandrasekaran advised treating every AI agent like a new engineering hire. Organizations should grant agents distinct non-human identities, implement tiered access controls distinguishing read-only operations from reversible write actions, version third-party Model Context Protocol (MCP) dependencies, and strictly isolate API secrets outside the agent's runtime environment in sandboxes. Ultimately, while engineering, security, and privacy teams validate safety guardrails, deployment approval remains a strategic business decision.

entries.title: Grafana Applies SLOs and Error Budgets to AI Agent Behaviour
entries.summary: Grafana Labs is proposing a familiar reliability engineering approach for one of the less familiar problems in modern software: how to measure whether an AI agent is actually behaving well. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
Grafana Labs is proposing a familiar reliability engineering approach for one of the less familiar problems in modern software: how to measure whether an AI agent is actually behaving well. In a recent article, the company describes using evaluations, service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets to turn behaviours such as hallucination, task fulfilment, toxicity, and cost into measurable targets that can be monitored over time.

The idea addresses a fundamental limitation of conventional application observability. Traditional metrics can tell engineers that an agent responded quickly, encountered no technical errors, and consumed a certain number of tokens, but none necessarily indicate whether its answer was correct, grounded in available information, or useful to the user. Grafana's approach is to evaluate the behaviour itself and turn the result into an SLI that can be measured against an SLO.

The first step is evaluation. An evaluation examines an agent interaction and determines whether it met a particular behavioural criterion. Grafana describes examples including whether a response was grounded in its supplied context, fulfilled the user's request, contained toxic content, exposed personal information, or succumbed to prompt injection. Evaluations can use another language model as a judge, but deterministic checks such as regular expressions can also be used where the behaviour can be identified without an LLM.

This is an important distinction from trying to create a single "agent quality score." Grafana argues that quality is multidimensional: an agent might be well grounded but expensive, helpful but occasionally toxic, or accurate but slow. Treating these as separate measurements allows teams to establish different objectives for the behaviours that matter to a particular application rather than hiding important failures inside an aggregate score.

Once a behaviour can be measured, conventional SRE concepts become applicable. Grafana gives the example of setting an SLO requiring 95% of conversations to be judged as fulfilled over 30 days. The remaining 5% becomes the error budget: the amount of unacceptable behaviour the team has explicitly decided it can tolerate within that period.

This approach matters less for the percentage itself than for the decision-making model it creates. When sufficient error budget remains, teams can experiment with prompts, models, or agent behaviour. As the budget is consumed, the priority can shift towards improving quality rather than introducing additional changes. This is conceptually the same trade-off SRE teams have long used to balance reliability against development velocity. Grafana's existing SLO tooling similarly defines an SLO through an SLI, target, and time window, with the error budget calculated from the gap between the target and 100%.

The approach becomes particularly useful when agent behaviour changes gradually rather than failing dramatically. A conventional alert might identify a sudden spike in failed requests, but an agent can continue responding successfully while its answers become subtly less useful. A model change, prompt modification, retrieval change, or shift in user behaviour might cause quality to deteriorate by a fraction of a percentage point each day.

Grafana argues that monitoring error-budget burn can make this type of drift visible. A single poor interaction may not matter against a 30-day objective, but a persistent decline can steadily consume the available budget. That provides a different signal from traditional infrastructure monitoring: the concern is not necessarily whether one execution failed, but whether the aggregate behaviour of the system is moving outside an agreed reliability envelope.

The hardest part may not be creating the SLO, but deciding what constitutes acceptable behaviour. Unlike availability targets, where organisations have decades of operational experience to draw upon, there is considerably less consensus around whether an agent should achieve 85%, 95% or 99% fulfilment or groundedness.

Grafana's approach is to establish a baseline through evaluations and then use historical results to help recommend an appropriate target. The target can subsequently be tightened as the agent matures. The concept also reflects a broader change in what observability needs to cover. Grafana's own Agent Observability work grew from the problem of monitoring its Grafana Assistant as prompt, model, and tool changes made traditional monitoring insufficient. In community discussions, Grafana engineers have distinguished between offline evaluations, which validate changes against known scenarios, and online evaluations, which assess behaviour against real production interactions.

Traditional observability generally asks whether the system is available and performing within technical limits. AI systems introduce another layer: whether the system's decisions and outputs remain within acceptable behavioural boundaries. That creates a feedback loop between evaluation, observability, and engineering change that more closely resembles continuous quality measurement than conventional application monitoring.

There is also an important limitation. An SLO is only as useful as the measurement underneath it. If an LLM judge consistently misclassifies responses, the resulting error budget may provide a false sense of precision. Similarly, a poorly designed evaluation can reward an agent for producing outputs that technically satisfy a criterion while failing to satisfy the user's actual intent.

This means organisations still need representative evaluation datasets, clear definitions of acceptable behaviour, appropriate deterministic checks where possible, human review for ambiguous cases, and ongoing validation of the evaluators themselves. The SLO provides the governance mechanism, but it does not make the underlying quality measurement inherently correct.

SLOs have traditionally provided a common language for engineering teams to balance reliability and change: define what matters, measure it, establish an acceptable threshold, and use the remaining error budget to guide decisions.

>Applying the same thinking to AI agents extends that model from system reliability to behavioural reliability. An agent can be technically available while being operationally unreliable because its answers are increasingly inaccurate, ungrounded, expensive, or unsafe. Treating those behaviours as measurable service objectives gives engineering teams a mechanism for detecting that degradation and deciding when experimentation should give way to remediation.

The significance is therefore not simply that Grafana has added another AI metric. It is that a mature SRE principle is being adapted to an environment where the system can remain "up" while becoming progressively less trustworthy. For organisations moving AI agents into production, that distinction may become one of the more important parts of AI observability.

Grafana's SLO approach is part of a broader industry effort to make agent behaviour measurable, although other organisations are approaching the problem from different directions. Anthropic, for example, has developed more formal evaluation practices for agents, using defined tasks, repeated trials and multiple graders to measure whether an agent consistently achieves its intended outcome. Its distinction between pass@k, which measures whether an agent succeeds at least once across multiple attempts, and pass^k, which measures whether it succeeds consistently across all attempts, is particularly relevant to production agents where reliability matters more than finding an answer eventually.

OpenTelemetry is approaching the problem at a different layer, working on standardised semantic conventions for agent telemetry so that traces, metrics and logs can provide a consistent basis for evaluating agent behaviour across frameworks and vendors. Together, these approaches illustrate an emerging pattern: evaluations determine whether an agent behaved correctly, observability provides the evidence, and SLOs provide the operational threshold for deciding whether that behaviour is acceptable.

entries.title: Mini book: Evolutionary Architecture in Practice
entries.summary: Discover how to keep software evolvable as systems, technology, and teams shift. This edition explores agentic fitness functions for semantic drift, treating human comprehension as a core design metric, cross-cloud guardrails for regional autonomy, and aligning technical boundaries with Conway’s Law. Move beyond static diagrams to continuous feedback systems that keep change safe and intentional.
entries.content:
Architecture is often framed as simply making change easier. A far more compelling argument is that evolution is about keeping change safe, clear, and deliberate in the face of constant technological and organizational movement.

Together, these articles offer much more than another collection of architectural patterns - they present evolutionary architecture as a continuous feedback system. Fitness functions signal when a system drifts; comprehension confirms people still grasp what they are modifying; boundaries define where independent change can happen; platforms turn safe practices into repeatable defaults; and organizational design ensures those boundaries actually survive contact with reality.

Free download

The InfoQ Evolutionary Architecture in Practice eMag includes:

The articles in this eMag were written by participants of the online InfoQ Certified Architect Program. They represent the capstone of their work, reflecting the cohort's collective learnings on the intersection of AI and modern software architecture.

  • Agentic Fitness Functions: Extending Evolutionary Architecture Beyond Deterministic Rules by Hemant Kumar Mahato, Łukasz Sieczkowski , Vijaysenthilkumar Kuppusamy

    This article explores how agentic fitness functions extend evolutionary architecture beyond deterministic rules. It describes a governed AI judgment layer that evaluates semantic drift, boundary fidelity, and architectural risks inside CI/CD workflows, helping software architects, senior developers, and engineering leaders protect system integrity at speed without slowing down delivery.

  • Comprehension as an Architectural Characteristic: A System That Is Not Understood Cannot Evolve Safely by Jacobus Meintjes, Narayana Rengaswamy, Paul Katsande, Sureshbabu Bikki

    As AI commoditizes code output, system comprehension silently decays, creating cognitive debt that threatens safe architectural evolution. This article explores why human understanding must be treated as an essential architectural characteristic, offering actionable strategies, socio-technical metrics, and design checkpoints to preserve intent across modern engineering teams.

  • Fitness Functions and Team Boundaries: Lessons from Evolving a B2C Platform for B2B by Devora Roth Goldshmidt, Dmitry Kekelidze, Hassan Ejaz, Ifiok Idiang, Sebastian Hans

    This article explores how evolutionary architecture keeps systems maintainable using fitness functions and domain alignment. Through a real-world B2C-to-B2B expansion, it covers database schema evolution, backward-compatible API changes across team boundaries, and refactoring service boundaries - offering key insights for senior software developers, software architects, and engineering leaders.

  • Evolutionary Architecture Across Clouds and Regions: How Platform Guardrails Enable Regional Autonomy by Andrey Morozov, Khooviraj Seewoonauth, Mark-Oliver Masur, Maylin Leal, Swetha Iyengar

    This article explores how platform guardrails, fitness functions, and domain boundaries enable evolutionary architecture across multi-cloud and regional environments. Designed for senior software developers, architects, and engineering leaders, it balances regional autonomy with centralized security, compliance, and observability without central lock-in.

  • Evolving the Vibed Prototype: A Distributed Architecture Path to Production Without a Rewrite by Federico Briano, Michele Torello, Yuri Diamanti

    This article explores how engineering leaders can evolve AI-assisted prototypes into distributed systems without a complete rewrite. It describes a strategic, three-phase framework driven by domain boundaries, platform golden paths, and automated governance - enabling teams to slash lead times and cognitive load while balancing rapid innovation with long-term architectural stability.
  • Evolutionary Architecture Through Conway's Law: Federating Ownership Without Losing Coherence by Gururaj Raghavendra, Max Knee, Zahir Mansuri

    This article explores how evolutionary architecture and Conway's Law enable engineering leaders to federate system ownership without losing coherence. It describes actionable strategies for shifting from centralized services to autonomous lines of business - leveraging the Inverse Conway Maneuver, zero-trust security, platform engineering, and micro-frontends to achieve true deployment independence.

This collection is particularly useful because none of the concerns exist in isolation. The interesting work happens in the connections between them, where architecture stops being a diagram of today's system and becomes a set of mechanisms that help it keep changing without losing coherence.

Thank you for reading! And, as always, please send any feedback to us at editors@infoq.com or on LinkedIn, Bluesky or X.

entries.title: Helidon 27 Introduces Restructured Programming Models and New Messaging and Data Modules
entries.summary: The release of Helidon 27 is the first release that follows the Oracle Tip & Tail Model of Library Development by which the Tip adopts the latest Java technology while the Tail provides a more stable and secure baseline. Concurrent with the release of JDK 27, new features in Helidon 27 include: an introduction to new major modules, Helidon Messaging and Helidon Data JDBC. By Michael Redlich
entries.content:
The release of Helidon 27 is the very first that follows the Oracle Tip & Tail Model of Library Development where the Tip adopts the latest Java technology and the Tail provides a more stable and secure baseline. Concurrent with the release of JDK 27, changes include a restructure of the original programming models and introduce two new modules, Helidon Messaging and Helidon Data JDBC.

Helidon 27 serves as the Tip, meaning that: it aligns with JDK 27; adopts the latest Java features; and will continue to be updated under the current OpenJDK release cadence. Therefore, Helidon 28 will be available with the upcoming release of JDK 28 in March 2027.

Helidon 4.5.5, still managed under the familiar Helidon semantic versioning, serves as the Tail, means that: it maintains Helidon 4.5 LTS on its JDK 21 baseline with support for JDK 25; prioritizes critical bugs, security fixes and carefully selected backports; and allows for a longer-lived production baseline for development teams.

Helidon 27 is maintained under the auspices of the Java Verified Portfolio (JVP), an ecosystem of Oracle-supported technologies first introduced at JavaOne 2026, It also includes JavaFX 27, Jipher 20 and the Java Platform Extension Visual Studio Code

Originally named J4C (Java for Cloud), Helidon was designed to be simple and fast, and originally contained two programming models: Helidon SE and Helidon MP. This release introduces the new Helidon Core, replacing Helidon SE, with two new programming models: Imperative and Declarative. As the names imply, Imperative, similar to heritage Helidon SE, allows developers to create their applications using “plain old” Java without dependency injection or annotations. Declarative, on the other hand, provides developers the ability to use dependency injection and annotations that generate imperative code and wiring at build time.

Helidon MicroProfile replaces the heritage Helidon MP and has been moved into its own project. It will continue to support the specifications under MicroProfile and Jakarta EE and follow the Helidon semantic versioning.

Helidon SE Integrations has also been moved to its own project and renamed as Helidon Extensions. Each extension will be independently maintained under their own release lifecycle.

Helidon Messaging, a new messaging layer that simplifies traditional messaging, avoids reactive APIs such as the MicroProfile Reactive Messaging specification. Developers can use ordinary, blocking Java for interoperability with connector-neutral channels, such as Kafka, JMS or Apache Pulsar, that are bound through configuration and pluggable connectors.

Helidon Data JDBC provides a unified API for working with data repository queries that serve as an abstraction over traditional Object–Relational Mapping (ORM). This enables interfaces with query definitions to be translated into implementation classes at compile time. Helidon Data JDBC supports the Jakarta Persistence specification and its corresponding implementations, EclipseLink and Hibernate ORM.

Introduced in September 2018, Helidon SE featured three core APIs to create a microservice -- a web server, configuration, and security -- for building microservices-based applications. Helidon MP implemented various MicroProfile specifications.

Helidon has evolved over the years with the Java community to include support for: GraalVM; Java Persistence Architecture (now Jakarta Persistence); Micronaut Data; Kotlin; MicroStream (now EclipseStore); and IntelliJ IDEA.

Released in June 2020, Helidon 2.0 introduced a web client (to complement the web server) and a database client in Helidon SE and a new command line tool (CLI).

Released in July 2022, Helidon 3.0 delivered: JDK 17 as a minimal version; an implementation of MicroProfile 5.0 and selected Jakarta EE 9.1 specifications; support for JEP 290, Filter Incoming Serialization Data, such that deserialization is disabled by default; an updated Helidon SE routing API; a new project starter; and an updated CLI.

The original Helidon web server, based on Netty, was available in the version 1.0 to 3.0 release trains. A new web server, codenamed Helidon Níma, was based on JEP 444, Virtual Threads, and introduced with the release of Helidon 4.0 in October 2023.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.0 and version 4.5.5.

entries.title: Presentation: Exploding GPUs
entries.summary: Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. By Andr
entries.content:
Transcript

Andrew Martin: The pithy version of this title, Exploding GPUs, is the hook. The issue is the AI Infrastructure Challenge. I'm here to convince you that AI security is still Kubernetes security, and then make a handful of caveats that may explode into an armful or a bucketful.

I'm Andy, founder and CEO of ControlPlane. We are cloud-native security engineering. For the last eight or so years, almost nine years, we have been working with regulated industries to secure next generation technologies. Ten years ago, that was taking Docker onto the public cloud. Then it became Kubernetes. The first regulated system we deployed was 1.2, which you may remember is no ABAC, no RBAC, no nothing. Since then, I've had the great pleasure of writing and training for O'Reilly, for SANS, and various other things for various other organizations. Securing the world's cloud-native infrastructure, focusing on regulated organizations with square peg round hole solutions for which there is generally no silver bullet. As you'll be pleased to know, this talk does not preach those things.

Outline

What will we look at? What are the challenges we see in AI security? How do these differ from what we have in Kubernetes fundamentally? What is the threat landscape? Of course, the amount of updates that this talk is required in days, weeks, barely months, to cover the rapidly evolving landscape is a constant update battle. MCP, agents, and mega-clusters, what happens when you've paid millions of dollars for thousands of GPUs? Then, finally, what do we actually do on Kubernetes? Fundamentally, every AI system is baselined on Kubernetes, OpenAI, Anthropic, whether they've built their own data centers, or whether they've had data centers built for them, or whether they're using burst capacity onto the public cloud. Everything there is running in a Kubernetes system of some type. There are some interesting deployments whereby OpenAI like to put as many containers into a single pod as possible, but almost blows up Kubernetes.

Whereas more generally, we'll talk about slightly saner patterns. We're inheriting the vulnerabilities of Kubernetes clusters with far higher value targets than we had before. We certainly have a new reputational risk. We don't want a chatbot to give our grandmother a ricin recipe, which from playing with chatbots, I'm sure you can tell, you can ask them for PhD level math equations, or with a jailbroken prompt, determine how to make a bomb, ricin. Your supply chain now includes your email, or a GitHub pull request title. We'll look at how supply chain attacks have evolved to bypass human review and to attack the model directly. Of course, OpenClaw made this an interesting little bit of research. We started off with Clawbot, which got ceased and desisted. Moltbot came in the middle. The word on the street is the gentleman who put this together, span up his own army of agents to get that insane virality curve that we saw at the beginning of the year. Kind of computes, why would you not do that? The fundamental problem here is that this threat landscape is very different to any of the threat models that we've contemplated before.

AI Security Challenges

You'll see Agent Smith from the Matrix percolating through the talk. Of course, he is one instant of an agent that scales horizontally, mutates, and is theoretically unconstrainable. In this case, he is the representative of these autonomous actors. We've suddenly gone from running a microservices galaxy, where we can predictably have user-driven contract testing, we can accept and test the distributed system to some extent. We can form those contracts and build up from unit tests, into a world of non-determinism, where we're looking for bounds testing and range checking for natural language answers. Don't believe the hype. This is not the way that many systems are doing things, and we'll look at how they should be secured. This concept of inheritance of risk. We'll look at how models like to break out of the things that they're put inside. Again, recent updates. GPU mega-clusters are the new crown jewels, and that's because instead of just crypto mining, as we used to, these keys are now valuable for threat actors who are running massive AI-driven campaigns.

If someone can get access to your GPU, they will broker that on the dark web, on the dark markets, and sell it to people who are spitting up tens of thousands of agents to try and attack web applications, run business email compromise campaigns, anything you can think of. Your GPU compute has become extremely valuable beyond crypto. Finally, we built a governance framework for FINOS, that is the Linux Foundation subsidiary, the FinTech Open-Source Organization. The architectures and pieces of work we've done in there have been validated by NVIDIA and OpenAI. It is the highest level of paranoia you can get, so pick and choose what makes sense for you from that framework. We'll go through and look at some of those things as we move forward. Broadly, it's only regulator-facing things that really differentiate, so I hope that provides a useful baseline when we get through the end of the talk.

Threat Landscape

What are we trying to protect? This is the SDLC for a machine learning system which is being trained. Banks, large organizations understand statistical models. They've been doing fraud detection. They've been doing prediction for many years. That's not really a problem. It's broadly how these things work. When we move into large language models, we have a different set of threats. Now, of course, the runtime threats of reputational damage or the incorrect or, frankly, IP, PII, or toxicity coming back from the endpoint as inference mean that most organizations will not actually be training end-to-end LLMs, but they'll still be using something akin to this for some form of fine-tuning. entries.title: AWS Introduces Strands Decider 2B and Strands Box for AI Agent Development
entries.summary: AWS has introduced two open-source projects for AI agent development: Strands Decider 2B, a small model designed to make decisions within agent workflows, and Strands Box, a sandbox for controlling agent execution. Both projects address different aspects of building agents that use tools, execute code, and interact with external systems. By Daniel Dominguez
entries.content:
AWS has introduced two open-source projects for AI agent development: Strands Decider 2B, a small model designed to make decisions within agent workflows, and Strands Box, a sandbox for controlling agent execution. Both projects address different aspects of building agents that use tools, execute code, and interact with external systems.

Strands Decider 2B is a two-billion-parameter model designed to select between predefined options rather than generate lengthy text responses. It supports tasks such as model routing, tool selection, classification, guardrails, and context management. Instead of asking a general-purpose language model to generate an answer, developers can provide a set of choices and receive a decision with confidence scores.

The model is based on Qwen3.5-2B, with its language-model head replaced by a pointer head that scores candidate answers. It uses a rank-16 LoRA adapter for fine-tuning. AWS has released the model weights, training data, and scripts, allowing developers to run and modify the model locally.

According to AWS, Strands Decider 2B achieved a median decision latency of approximately 115 milliseconds on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 and 153 milliseconds for small tasks on an Apple M3 MacBook. The company also evaluated the model using JevBench, reporting 72.3% accuracy across 231 public tasks for its v19 checkpoint. Developers can install the strands-decider package and use its command-line interface or integrate the model into Strands agents.

The second project, Strands Box, is available in developer preview and provides an isolated environment for executing AI agents. It combines operating-system-level isolation with Dogwood, an open-source policy language that defines which actions an agent can perform. The sandbox supports shell commands, Python execution, MCP tools, filesystem operations, and network access.

Strands Box uses kernel-enforced isolation to route agent interactions through a policy layer. Developers can allow or deny actions based on their content and execution history. For example, a policy can require an agent to pass tests before pushing code to a repository or restrict the frequency of external API calls. These controls operate outside the language model, reducing reliance on prompt instructions to enforce execution boundaries.

AWS says Strands Box can work with different models and agent frameworks, whether running locally or in cloud environments. This allows developers to introduce execution policies without replacing their existing agent architecture.

Strands Decider 2B competes with TypeSafe AI's Jev, another specialized model designed to make structured decisions without generating lengthy responses. Both support classification, routing, and tool selection, returning confidence scores alongside their decisions. The main difference is deployment: Strands Decider 2B is open source and can run locally, while Jev is available through a managed API. AWS evaluated Strands Decider using JevBench, although the published results do not establish a direct performance advantage over Jev.

Strands Box addresses problems also handled by container-based sandboxes, Firecracker microVMs, and hosted agent execution environments. While conventional sandboxing primarily restricts filesystem, process, and network access, Strands Box adds policies based on tool arguments and previous actions. This allows developers to define conditions that must be satisfied before an agent executes specific operations.

Early developer feedback has focused on the practical limitations of integrating small decision models into agent workflows. In a hands-on tutorial, AWS Community Builder Yuuki Yamashita reported that:

Strands Decider 2B could prevent an agent from making an unsupported weather-tool call.

GitHub discussions have also identified issues involving concurrent requests, Apple Silicon compatibility, and cold-start latency, highlighting areas developers may need to evaluate before using the model in production.

AI Builder Dipen Vaja commented on X:

I'd rather an agent hit a wall mid-run than finish a bad path. AWS open sourced Strands Box today: a kernel sandbox that routes shell, Python, tools and network through one policy layer, so a rule can block outbound HTTP after the agent reads a customer file.

Together, Strands Decider 2B and Strands Box extend the Strands ecosystem beyond agent orchestration into decision-making and execution control. The projects provide separate components for selecting agent actions and enforcing restrictions on how those actions are executed.

entries.title: Article: Cryptographic Foundation of Mobile ID Systems: An ISO/IEC 18013-5 Enterprise Architecture Blueprint
entries.summary: This article provides a framework for asking the right architectural questions before an enterprise commits to an mDL provider or library. It shows which components can be abstracted safely, which trust boundaries must remain visible to the enterprise, what cryptographic and interoperability properties should be verified, and how requirements change across real-world use cases. By Praveen Kumar Go
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • Decouple identity proofing from credential provisioning to establish clear architectural boundaries between identity verification and credential issuance.
  • Evaluate mobile driver’s license (mDL) providers by their underlying architecture, not just their APIs, including their integration patterns, security controls, and trust boundaries.
  • Use Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) for protected online identity transmission where appropriate, and design proximity presentations around standards-based NFC interactions.
  • Implement domain-specific selective disclosure to minimize the release of identity attributes while meeting individual verification requirements.
  • Treat the mDL provider as one component of a broader trust architecture, with explicit governance of trust boundaries extending beyond the provider’s SDK.

This article is intended for enterprise architects, security architects, identity engineers, platform leaders, technology evaluators, and product teams responsible for integrating or selecting mobile driver's license (mDL) capabilities. It is particularly relevant to organizations that will consume an mDL through a third-party provider, SDK, wallet platform, or verification service and therefore need to understand what is hidden behind the integration boundary.

This article provides a framework for asking the right architectural questions before an enterprise commits to an mDL provider or library. It shows which components can be abstracted safely, which trust boundaries must remain visible to the enterprise, what cryptographic and interoperability properties should be verified, and how requirements change across real-world use cases.

Introduction: The Mobile ID Integration Is Easy to Hide, Not Easy to Architect

The transition from physical credentials to digital Mobile Driver's Licenses represents more than a change in user interface. It changes where identity is stored, how identity claims are authenticated, how devices become trusted, how relying parties request information, and how verification works when network connectivity is unavailable.

An enterprise integrating an mDL may encounter an apparently simple developer experience:

Figure 1. mDL Provider SDK (Source: created by the author)

From the application's perspective, this may look like a handful of APIs, however the underlying architecture is considerably more complex:

Figure 2. Overall Mobile ID Architecture (Source: created by the author)

That abstraction is useful, but it creates a risk.

An enterprise does not necessarily need to implement every component itself. In many cases, using a specialized provider or library is the correct engineering decision. However, outsourcing implementation is not the same as outsourcing architectural responsibility.

A provider may successfully expose an API that provides operations like 

verifyCredential()
, 
requestPresentation()
, 
issueCredential()
, but the enterprise still needs to make several key decisions, including:
  • Where is the credential stored, and how is the device key protected?
  • Who controls the issuer trust anchors, and how are certificates validated and rotated?
  • How are credential validity and revocation handled, particularly when the verifier is offline?
  • Which identity attributes are disclosed, and can the enterprise enforce data-minimization policies?
  • What telemetry does the provider collect, and can presentation events be correlated to users?
  • What happens when the provider is unavailable, and can the enterprise migrate to another provider without redesigning the integration?

These questions are architectural requirements even when the corresponding functionality is implemented by someone else.

The architecture described in this article can therefore be used in two ways:

  • As an implementation blueprint for organizations building portions of an mDL ecosystem.
  • As an evaluation framework for organizations selecting an mDL provider, SDK, wallet platform, or verification library.

The second use is particularly important. A provider should not be evaluated solely by whether its SDK successfully completes a demonstration transaction. The enterprise should evaluate the trust model, cryptographic boundaries, interoperability, privacy controls, operational behavior, and failure modes hidden behind that SDK.

How This Article Approaches mDL Architecture

The article approaches Mobile ID as an enterprise architecture and trust-boundary problem rather than simply an SDK integration problem. It first separates identity proofing from credential provisioning, because these phases involve different actors, trust decisions, and security responsibilities. That distinction leads to the provider evaluation question: which responsibilities can be delegated to an mDL provider, and which trust decisions must remain visible to the enterprise? The article then introduces the credential structure and data model to show what is actually being provisioned and verified.

The article next follows the credential through a verification transaction. The high-level presentation flow establishes how the wallet, relying party, issuer trust, device authentication, and requested attributes interact. The following sections examine how that transaction is protected through cryptography, mTLS, and certificate infrastructure. The discussion then distinguishes operations requiring immediate availability from those that can run in the background, followed by offline operation and reconciliation to address provider, network, and trust-list failures.

The final sections examine how these principles change across relying-party use cases, how governance and privacy policies constrain implementation choices, and how enterprises can avoid excessive provider dependence while keeping important architectural decisions visible. The article brings these ideas together through an architecture review and a Build, Buy, and Govern decision model, helping enterprises determine which capabilities should remain under enterprise control and which can be delegated to specialized providers.

The goal is to connect these topics into a single architectural view: understand what is being trusted, what is being disclosed, how it is verified, what happens when connectivity or providers fail, and how the enterprise can continue to govern and change the implementation.

Who Should Read This Article?

The primary audience includes enterprise and solution architects who are deciding how mDL capabilities fit into an existing identity, API, mobile, security, and data architecture; security architects evaluating key management, device trust, certificate infrastructure, cryptographic boundaries, authentication, and privacy controls; identity and IAM engineers integrating mobile credentials with identity verification, relying-party applications, digital wallets, and enterprise identity platforms; technology and vendor evaluation teams evaluating commercial mDL providers, SDKs, verification platforms, wallet technologies, or managed identity services; engineering leaders who need to determine what should be built internally, what should be delegated to a provider, and what architectural controls must remain under enterprise ownership; and product and platform teams designing customer-facing applications where identity verification needs to operate across multiple environments, including online and offline scenarios.

For all of these audiences, the central question is not:

"Can this SDK verify an mDL?"

The more important question is:

"What trust, security, privacy, interoperability, and operational architecture exists behind the SDK, and does it satisfy the requirements of my enterprise?"

Proofing vs Provisioning Architecture

Proofing and provisioning are distinct phases in the credential lifecycle. Proofing validates that the user owns the identity claims, while provisioning establishes hardware trust, issues the encrypted payload, and installs the Mobile Security Object on the device.

Figure 3. Proofing and Provisioning Sequence (Source: created by the author.)

[Click here to expand image above to full-size]

Phase 1: Identity Proofing

Identity proofing consists of four main steps:

  • Identity Evidence Capture: The user captures images of their physical driver's license (front and back) along with a live facial video (liveness check) directly within the app.
  • Payload Submission: The collected images, extracted metadata, and liveness video are submitted to the verification system.
  • Authorization Check: The DMV or authoritative identity system evaluates the evidence using automated facial recognition against official records and manual review pipelines when necessary.
  • Proofing Decision: The verification engine returns an explicit status response: Approved or Rejected.

Phase 2: Identity Provisioning

Identity provisioning is carried through across four steps:

  • Hardware Key Generation: Upon receiving an Approved status, the wallet client requests the Secure Enclave or hardware security element to generate asymmetric device keys.
  • Attestation Bundle Assembly: The client extracts the generated device public key and hardware attestation X.509 certificates.
  • Provisioning Payload Submission: The wallet packages the device public key, public certificates, proofing reference ID, and device metadata, transmitting them to the issuer backend.
  • Credential Digesting and Encryption: The issuing authority digests the driver's license identity attributes, binds them to the device public key inside a signed Mobile Security Object, encrypts the credential bundle, and sends it back to the wallet.
  • Storage and Rendering: The wallet decrypts the incoming payload using session transport keys, writes the signed mSO data and keys into hardware-backed storage, and makes the credential available to display to the user.

An enterprise does not necessarily need to implement these nine steps itself. However, it should determine which party performs each step and which party controls the resulting trust decision.

A provider evaluation should therefore build a map to define who will supply each required function. For example:

Architectural FunctionEnterpriseProviderIssuer / DMVShared / External
Identity proofing✓
Device key generation✓ / SDK
Device attestation✓
Credential issuance✓
Document signing✓
Wallet storage✓ / Device
Presentation✓ / App✓ / SDK
Verification✓ / RP✓ / Service
Trust management✓✓✓
Revocation/status✓✓✓
Audit and telemetry✓✓✓

The exact ownership model will vary, but the enterprise should be able to explain the trust boundary rather than simply accepting the provider's default abstraction.

What an Enterprise Should Ask an mDL Provider

A black-box integration can be appropriate for implementation, but it is insufficient for architectural due diligence.

An enterprise evaluating an mDL provider should ensure that the provider can clearly explain six areas:

  • Cryptographic architecture: Key generation and protection, device attestation, algorithms, signatures, and key lifecycle.
  • Trust and PKI: Trust anchors, Document Signer certificates, trust lists, revocation, and certificate lifecycle.
  • Privacy and data minimization: Selective disclosure, telemetry, presentation-data retention, location information, and correlation risks.
  • Offline operation: Cached trust material, revocation/status synchronization, stale information, and behavior during network disruption.
  • Interoperability: ISO/IEC 18013-5 compliance, independent wallet and verifier interoperability, standardized data structures, and provider portability.
  • Operational resilience: provider dependencies, outage behavior, credential continuity, recovery, and failure handling.

The objective is not to eliminate abstraction. The objective is to ensure that the abstraction hides implementation complexity without hiding architectural risk.

A detailed provider due-diligence checklist is provided in Appendix A.

Credential Structure and Data Model

ISO/IEC 18013-5 uses structured, compact data representations to carry issuer-signed identity claims. The credential contains issuer-signed namespaces, element identifiers, digests, issuer authentication, device key information, and validity information.

The architectural significance is that the enterprise does not simply receive "identity data." It receives cryptographically structured claims whose authenticity and integrity depend on issuer signatures, value digests, device keys, and the surrounding trust infrastructure.

A representative credential structure is provided in Appendix B, including the relationship between issuer-signed data, the Mobile Security Object (mSO), device authentication, and credential validity.

This distinction also affects how an enterprise evaluates an mDL provider or library. The integration should not be assessed solely on whether it can parse or deserialize the credential payload. It must also expose and correctly enforce the security properties represented by that payload.

The enterprise should therefore establish whether the implementation:

  • validates issuer signatures correctly;
  • validates the Mobile Security Object;
  • validates device authentication;
  • validates certificate chains;
  • supports selective disclosure;
  • protects sensitive credential material;
  • exposes sufficient verification results to the application;
  • and preserves standards-based interoperability.

From Credential Structure to Enterprise Verification

Understanding the credential structure is only the first step. The enterprise must also understand how that credential is presented, protected, verified, and governed across online and offline environments.

The following sections trace those concerns through the verification lifecycle, from presentation and cryptographic protection to trust infrastructure, availability, offline reconciliation, and enterprise policy.

High Level User Presentation Flow

Figure 4. User Presentation Flow (Source: created by the author)

The presentation flow illustrates how an mDL moves from the user's wallet to a relying party during a verification transaction. The verifier initiates a presentation request, the wallet establishes the appropriate secure communication channel, the user authorizes the requested disclosure, and the verifier validates the resulting credential data, issuer trust, device authentication, and applicable policy.

The flow provides the operational context for the architectural topics that follow. The subsequent sections examine the security mechanisms supporting this transaction including cryptographic protection, certificate and trust infrastructure, synchronous and asynchronous interactions, and offline and reconciliation behavior and show how these mechanisms affect enterprise integration and provider evaluation.

Security and Cryptography: HPKE Integration

Hybrid Public Key Encryption defined in RFC 9180 secures online transmissions and direct API exchanges between verifiers and wallet servers. HPKE combines asymmetric key encapsulation mechanisms with symmetric authenticated encryption with associated data to yield low latency encryption.

Figure 5. Payload Encryption Sequence (Source: created by the author.)

HPKE Parameters

  • KEM: DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) (ID: 0x0010)
  • KDF: HKDF-SHA256 (ID: 0x0001)
  • AEAD: AES-128-GCM (ID: 0x0001)

The key architectural point is that encryption should be considered part of a broader trust model rather than a standalone security feature.

When evaluating an mDL provider, ask:

Does the provider merely advertise "encrypted communication", or can it explain the cryptographic boundary, key lifecycle, algorithm selection, key storage, and endpoint authentication?

A provider should be able to document:

  • where encryption begins;
  • where encryption terminates;
  • which keys are generated by the device;
  • which keys are generated by backend systems;
  • how keys are protected;
  • how key rotation works;
  • and which components are within the provider's trust boundary.

Encryption without a clearly understood trust boundary can create a false sense of security.

Mutual TLS (mTLS) and Certificate Infrastructure

Server-to-server communications between wallet servers, issuer platforms, and verifier systems require mutual TLS authentication alongside PKI validation.

Figure 6. mTLS Channel (Source: created by the author.)

The trust topology relies on specialized certificate types

Figure 7. Trust Topology (Source: created by the author.)

Certificate TypePurposeLifetimeKey TypeStorage Location
Root Trust AnchorEstablishes root identity hierarchy10 to 20 yearsECDSA P-384 / RSA 4096Offline HSM
Issuing Authority CASigns state specific issuing keys3 to 5 yearsECDSA P-256High Security HSM
Document SignerSigns short lived identity structures30 to 90 daysECDSA P-256Online HSM
mTLS Client / ServerAuthenticates inter-system API connections1 yearRSA 3072 / ECDSA P-256API Gateway Key Vault
Verifier Reader CertAuthenticates Relying Party terminals1 yearECDSA P-256Secure Hardware
Device Attestation CertValidates device key authenticity1 to 3 yearsECDSA P-256Device Secure Element

The important question for an enterprise is not necessarily whether the provider operates this infrastructure itself.

The question is:

Which certificate infrastructure does the provider operate, which does the enterprise operate, and which trust relationships remain under the issuing authority's control?

The provider should be able to explain certificate lifecycle management, certificate rotation, trust-anchor management, failure behavior, and responsibilities during certificate compromise.

Synchronous vs Asynchronous Operations

An enterprise mDL architecture does not use a single interaction pattern for every operation. Some activities must complete within the user-facing verification transaction, while others can occur in the background without delaying credential presentation. The architectural objective is therefore not to choose synchronous or asynchronous processing as a single model, but to identify which operations require immediate availability and which can tolerate delay, caching, or eventual synchronization.

This distinction matters particularly when an enterprise relies on an external mDL provider. If a provider becomes unavailable, the impact depends on which operations are coupled to that provider at runtime. A well-designed architecture should allow existing credentials and offline verification to continue where the applicable trust and policy requirements permit, while allowing operations such as issuance, provisioning, online verification, and trust-list synchronization to depend on backend availability where necessary.

Synchronous Real-Time Exchanges

In-person scanning: Near Field Communication (NFC) transfer. The verifier reader initiates a tap engagement over NFC, establishes the session keys, requests specific identity namespaces, and receives the signed payload response directly over the secure NFC channel.

Direct API verification: Online transactions query the wallet verification API directly. The verifier sends a presentation request, the user authenticates, and data returns within a single HTTP request-response cycle.

Asynchronous Background Processes

Identity proofing evaluation: Identity evidence verification, including manual review or DMV record lookup, can run asynchronously. The client receives a callback or polling update once the result is available.

Push provisioning: Following proofing approval, asynchronous notifications can trigger wallet key generation and final credential delivery.

Key rotation and trust-list synchronization: Verifiers can obtain updated trust material and revocation information through background synchronization rather than requiring these updates to occur during every presentation transaction.

Architectural Implication

The enterprise should explicitly map each operation to its availability requirement:

OperationShould Provider Outage Prevent It?
Existing offline credential presentationIdeally no
Offline credential verificationIdeally no
Credential issuancePotentially yes
Online verificationPotentially yes
Trust-list synchronizationCan be deferred
Credential revocation updateCan be temporarily deferred according to policy
New credential provisioningPotentially yes

The purpose of this classification is to identify runtime provider dependencies and failure boundaries. An enterprise should not assume that because a provider is highly available, every mDL transaction should depend on that provider being reachable.

A provider can be highly available and still create an architectural single point of failure if every verification transaction requires its online infrastructure. Conversely, an architecture that deliberately separates user-facing verification from background synchronization can preserve critical verification capabilities during temporary provider or network outages.

Reconciliation and Offline Considerations

State changes must sync across systems while maintaining user privacy.

Figure 8. Reconciliation Topology (Source: created by the author.)

Synchronization Under Network Disruption

  • Offline Verifiers: Terminals cache Document Signer certificates and revocation lists. Scans execute purely over local NFC. Data syncs to central cloud logs once network access restores.
  • Device Expiry Enforcement: The mSO payload includes validFrom and validUntil timestamps. If an offline phone's secure clock exceeds validUntil, the reader rejects the credential.

Offline capability should be one of the most important evaluation criteria for an mDL provider.

A provider demonstration conducted entirely over a high-speed internet connection does not demonstrate offline readiness.

A serious evaluation should ask the provider to demonstrate:

  • Credential presentation without network connectivity.
  • Verification without network connectivity.
  • Cached trust material.
  • Expired credential behavior.
  • Stale revocation information.
  • Network restoration.
  • Synchronization after reconnection.
  • Device clock anomalies.
  • Provider outage behavior.

The objective is to test the failure architecture, not just the happy path.

Specialized Use Cases

Although mDL verification shares a common foundation, relying parties differ in assurance requirements, requested attributes, operational constraints, and privacy expectations. The following examples illustrate these differences: comprehensive identity verification at airports versus minimal disclosure for retail age verification.

Figure 9. Verification Request Routing (Source: created by the author.)

Airline Security Checkpoints

Figure 10. TSA Verification Sequence (Source: created by the author.)

Airports require full identity verification against passenger manifests.

  • Requested Attributes: Given name, family name, photograph, birth date, document number, issuing authority, and real ID compliance flag.
  • Operational Integration: TSA readers extract attributes, verify the Document Signer certificate against federal trust lists, and perform biometric face matching.

Liquor Store Age Verification

Figure 11. Store Verification Sequence (Source: created by the author.)

Retail environments require fast verification with minimal data exposure.

  • Requested Attributes: age_over_21 boolean and user portrait.
  • Data Minimization: Name, address, document number, and birth date are omitted from the data payload.
  • Operational Integration: The terminal validates the cryptographic signature, displays the portrait on the screen, and shows an age-approved status indicator.

Operational Integration

The terminal validates the cryptographic signature, verifies the required claims, displays the portrait where appropriate, and produces an age-approved status.

The architectural priority is data minimization and transaction simplicity.

These two examples illustrate why an enterprise should not evaluate an mDL provider based on a single demonstration.

An implementation optimized for airport identity verification may expose more data than a retail application requires.

Conversely, a provider optimized for simple age verification may not expose the controls required for high-assurance identity verification.

The provider must therefore be evaluated against the enterprise's actual relying-party policies and transaction classes.

Governance, Compliance, and Technical Policies

Governance, privacy, security, and interoperability requirements shape how mDL systems request attributes, retain information, manage cryptographic material, and enforce standards. The following policies translate these requirements into controls for enterprise applications and third-party providers.

  • Data Minimization Mandate: Verifier software must request only elements necessary for the transaction. Storing PII by commercial verifiers is prohibited unless regulatory exceptions apply.
  • Zero Tracking Guarantee: Issuing authorities must not build provisioning or status systems that track when or where a user presents their credential.
  • Cryptographic Hygiene: Document Signer keys must rotate every 30 to 90 days. Systems must use SHA-256 or SHA-384 cryptographic primitives.
  • Hardware Key Binding Enforcement: Apps must configure keys with biometric or PIN user authentication requirements inside secure hardware.
  • Interoperability Compliance: All wallet software and verifiers must certify compliance with ISO/IEC 18013-5 standards.

Avoiding Vendor Lock-In

An mDL provider can reduce implementation complexity, but excessive abstraction can create long-term dependency.

For example:

Figure 12. Provider SDK (Source: created by the author.)

This architecture may be convenient but difficult to replace.

A more resilient architecture places a standards-oriented abstraction boundary between the enterprise and provider:

Figure 13. Mobile ID Enterprise Application (Source: created by the author.)

The enterprise should not necessarily implement the protocol itself.

Instead, it should avoid allowing provider-specific implementation details to become inseparable from business logic.

For example, application code should ideally express:

RequestAgeOver21()

rather than embedding provider-specific credential structures throughout the application.

Similarly, verification results should be normalized into enterprise policy decisions rather than exposing proprietary provider responses throughout the application.

This architecture allows the provider to remain replaceable while preserving the business application's independence.

What Should Remain Visible Behind the Abstraction?

A useful rule for enterprise architecture is:

Hide implementation complexity, but expose architectural decisions.

An mDL SDK can appropriately hide:

  • CBOR serialization;
  • APDU construction;
  • cryptographic library invocation;
  • low-level NFC session handling;
  • platform-specific secure storage APIs.

However, the enterprise should retain visibility into:

  • trust anchors;
  • credential issuer identity;
  • verification outcome;
  • disclosed attributes;
  • certificate status;
  • credential validity;
  • revocation/status state;
  • provider dependencies;
  • privacy and telemetry behavior;
  • offline capabilities;
  • security boundaries;
  • and failure conditions.

This distinction makes the provider integration easier to operate without turning the provider into an opaque trust authority.

Architecture Review Before Production

Before production, enterprises must validate an mDL integration's trust boundaries, privacy, security, resilience, and interoperability, not merely successful verification. The following five questions provide a practical framework for reviewing these responsibilities and assessing provider dependencies.

1. What do we trust?

Identify:

  • issuer;
  • wallet;
  • device;
  • provider;
  • verifier;
  • certificate authorities;
  • trust lists;
  • backend services.

2. What do we disclose?

Map every relying-party transaction to the minimum required attributes.

3. What happens offline?

Document exactly which functions continue operating without connectivity.

4. What happens when something fails?

Test:

  • expired credentials;
  • invalid signatures;
  • invalid device authentication;
  • revoked certificates;
  • stale trust lists;
  • provider outage;
  • network outage;
  • device compromise;
  • synchronization failure.

5. Can we change providers?

Determine whether the enterprise can replace the SDK or provider without rewriting application business logic or changing its identity policy model.

These questions provide an architecture review framework that is useful even when the enterprise never implements the underlying cryptographic components itself.

A Practical Decision Model for Enterprise Adoption

An enterprise can classify mDL capabilities into three categories.

Build

Capabilities that represent strategic enterprise policy or trust decisions, including:

  • transaction-specific disclosure policies;
  • enterprise authorization rules;
  • application-level identity policy;
  • audit requirements;
  • integration orchestration.

Buy

Capabilities where specialized providers offer significant implementation advantages, including:

  • wallet SDKs;
  • protocol implementations;
  • NFC stack integration;
  • cryptographic libraries;
  • credential verification services.

Govern

Capabilities that may be operated by a provider but must remain subject to enterprise oversight, including:

  • key management;
  • certificate infrastructure;
  • device attestation;
  • revocation;
  • telemetry;
  • privacy;
  • availability;
  • interoperability.

This model avoids two extremes. The first is attempting to build every component internally. The second is treating the entire identity system as an opaque third-party service. The more appropriate enterprise approach is:

Buy implementation efficiency. Build enterprise policy. Govern the trust boundary.

A Thought-Provoking Question for Readers and Identity Architects

If mobile identity verification moves toward a cryptographically bound, privacy-preserving, offline-capable model, how can issuing authorities and commercial relying parties reconcile strict regulatory audit requirements with modern privacy laws that discourage unnecessary retention of sensitive personal information?

A related architectural question is:

How can issuing authorities, providers, and relying parties maintain privacy-preserving revocation and status checking without introducing new mechanisms for tracking where and when users present their mobile identities?

These questions remain important because cryptographic correctness alone does not guarantee privacy.

A technically valid identity system can still create privacy risk through telemetry, centralized status checking, excessive data retention, or poorly designed provider integrations.

Conclusion

The evolution of digital identity from physical cards to ISO/IEC 18013-5-compliant Mobile Driver's Licenses represents a fundamental transformation in enterprise trust models.

The most important architectural lesson is not that every enterprise should implement the entire mDL stack itself.

It is that enterprises need to understand the architecture they are buying, even when they are not building it.

A provider or SDK can appropriately abstract away CBOR encoding, NFC APDU handling, cryptographic library calls, secure storage APIs, and other implementation details. But the enterprise still needs to understand who controls the issuer trust, how device keys are protected, how selective disclosure is enforced, how revocation works, what happens offline, what information is collected, and how the system behaves when a provider becomes unavailable.

High-speed NFC presentation, hardware-backed device keys, cryptographic signatures, HPKE, PKI, selective disclosure, and offline verification are not isolated technical features. They are interconnected parts of an enterprise trust model.

The strongest architecture is therefore not necessarily the one with the most sophisticated provider or the largest number of APIs.

It is the one where the enterprise can clearly answer: Who do we trust? What are we disclosing? How do we verify it? What happens when we are offline? What happens when a provider fails? And can we change the implementation without changing our trust model?

By treating mDL integration as an architecture and governance problem rather than simply an SDK integration problem, enterprises can adopt vendor capabilities while retaining control over security, privacy, interoperability, and long-term technology strategy.

Appendix A — mDL Provider Architecture Due-Diligence Checklist

A provider or library should be evaluated across at least six dimensions.

Cryptographic Architecture

Ask:

  • Which algorithms are supported?
  • Where are private keys generated?
  • Are device keys hardware-backed?
  • How is device attestation validated?
  • How are issuer signatures validated?
  • How are cryptographic keys rotated?
  • What happens when certificates expire?
  • Which cryptographic libraries are used?
  • Can cryptographic configuration be independently audited?

Trust and PKI

Ask:

  • Who controls the trust anchors?
  • How are Document Signer certificates validated?
  • How are Master Lists handled?
  • How are Certificate Revocation Lists distributed?
  • How frequently are trust lists updated?
  • Can the verifier operate with cached trust information?
  • How are trust-anchor changes distributed?

Privacy and Data Minimization

Ask:

  • Can the relying party request individual attributes?
  • Can the application enforce transaction-specific disclosure policies?
  • Does the provider retain presentation data?
  • Does the provider collect location information?
  • Can telemetry be disabled or minimized?
  • Can presentation events be correlated to users?
  • Where is PII processed and stored?

Offline Operation

Ask:

  • Can the credential be verified without network access?
  • Which trust material must be cached?
  • How are certificate and status updates synchronized?
  • What happens when status information is stale?
  • What happens when the device clock is incorrect?
  • Can the provider demonstrate verification during network disruption?

Interoperability

Ask:

  • Does the implementation support ISO/IEC 18013-5?
  • Can it interoperate with independently implemented wallets?
  • Can it interoperate with independently implemented verifiers?
  • Does the provider support standardized data structures?
  • Are proprietary extensions clearly separated from standards-based functionality?
  • Can the enterprise migrate away from the provider?

Operational Resilience

Ask:

  • What happens if the provider's API is unavailable?
  • Can credential presentation continue?
  • Can existing credentials continue operating?
  • What provider dependencies exist at runtime?
  • What provider dependencies exist during issuance?
  • What happens during certificate or trust-list outages?
  • What is the recovery model?

The objective is not to eliminate abstraction.

The objective is to make sure the abstraction hides implementation complexity without hiding architectural risk.
